expectations_used.clarify: Establishes what the failing assertion is actually comparing before editing — that one side is the snapshot-accelerated read and the other is a full replay of the same log — and asks or states which of the two is the trusted reference.
expectations_used.approach: Names a mechanism, not a location: says something like 'the snapshot boundary event is being folded twice' or 'the replay range overlaps the snapshot' rather than 'the bug is in the snapshot code' or 'something is wrong with balances'.
expectations_used.communicate: Narrates the reasoning while navigating the ledger module — which account is off, by how much, and which single event's amount that difference matches — instead of scrolling and editing in silence.
expectations_used.implement: Changes only the boundary of the replay range so events after the snapshot are folded once, and leaves the snapshot writer, the event log, and the guard clauses on deposits, withdrawals and transfers untouched.
expectations_used.verify: Reruns the whole suite after the edit and checks that the previously failing case now agrees with reconcile, rather than declaring the fix done from reading the diff, and confirms no other test regressed.
expectations_used.reflect: States why the failure only surfaced once the log grew past the snapshot interval — shorter ledgers have no snapshot to resolve through — and what that implies about the tests that were passing all along.

summary: The candidate spent the entire 7-minute session reading test output and navigating the ledger module — event class, append, snapshot resolution — without ever forming or stating a concrete hypothesis about the bug. They got close to the actual defect (reading the self.snapshot minus one/sequence line near the end) but asked for a hint rather than reasoning it through, and the session ended before any code was changed or the failing test was rerun.</summary>

dimensions.analysis: The candidate read the failure output and noted the specific numbers (Alice 450 vs expected value) but never articulated which side of the assertion was the trusted reference (full replay) versus the accelerated path (snapshot read). They spent minutes manually trying to hand-compute the expected balance rather than stating what the two things being compared actually represented, which is the core ambiguity this problem posed.

No mechanism was ever named. The candidate drifted from guessing about fees, to self-transfer guards, to append internals, to snapshot code, without ever committing to a hypothesis like 'the boundary event is folded twice'. Even after reading the snapshot-resolution code around minus-one/sequence, they did not state what the line meant or why it might be wrong before asking for a hint.

There is substantial narration of what code they were looking at (event class, append, balances), but it is mostly reading code aloud rather than reasoning about why — long silent 'Um' stretches punctuate the transcript and the interviewer had to intervene twice to ask for their actual theory, indicating the transcript alone would not explain their path.

The candidate never made a code edit during the session — all activity was file navigation and reading. The session ended with them still asking for a hint about the snapshot boundary line, before any implementation was attempted.
No fix was implemented and no test was rerun after the initial failing run at the start, so there was nothing to verify.

The session ended before any resolution or root-cause statement was reached; the candidate was still requesting a hint on the exact snapshot line (self.snapshot minus one, sequence) when they ended the session, so no explanation of the mechanism was ever given.
